where: Section 2, the paragraph explaining why the holder must not sleep
problem: The sentence 'Sleeping means calling schedule(), which can switch to another task that wants the same lock; the holder is then not running, so nobody releases it' is loose. A sleeping holder usually does release the lock later; the real trouble is that every other CPU keeps spinning (wasting cycles) and, if the wake-up itself needs that lock, the system deadlocks. As written a student may think any sleep inside a spinlock is an instant permanent deadlock, or may miss the 'other CPUs waste cycles' reason.
fix: Rewrite: 'The holder must never sleep. While it sleeps the lock stays taken, so every other CPU that wants it spins and burns cycles, and if the event that would wake the holder needs the same lock the spinning CPUs deadlock. So keep spinlocked sections to a few instructions.'

problem: 'the count is 0 or 1' is incomplete and slightly misleading: in Linux an unlocked mutex has count 1, a locked mutex has count 0, and the count goes negative when tasks are waiting. A student may also read '0 or 1' as 'up to two holders'.
fix: Say: 'the count is 1 when free and 0 when taken, and it goes negative to record waiters; it never exceeds 1, so only one holder at a time.'

problem: 'A completion is a one-shot signal' can mislead. A completion counts complete() calls and is reusable: if complete(&c) runs before wait_for_completion(&c), the wait returns immediately instead of blocking, and the same completion object can be used again.
fix: Say: 'A completion is a counter with a wait queue: wait_for_completion(&c) blocks only if no complete(&c) has been counted yet; a complete() that arrives first makes the next wait return at once, and the object can be reused.'
